items.question: How do you frame your lab’s research agenda for trustworthy AI systems?
items.object: Research agenda for trustworthy AI systems
items.answer: My lab broadly is interested in trustworthy AI systems. We think both about foundations: what does it mean to think about measurement and assessment? What are the gaps in current systems? Then we think about mitigation: what can we do, and what are the tools that we can bring to bear to help close trustworthiness gaps in building AI systems once deployed?

items.question: How has your attitude toward working on language research changed since graduate school?
items.object: Engaging with language research as a machine learning researcher
items.answer:
My students definitely got bit by the bug and, maybe initially a bit kicking and screaming, pulled me into thinking about language much more. I've found it fascinating. Weirdly, I avoided language as a grad student. I remember distinctly going to some of these shared cross-lab meetings that had folks from Cornell, like I was, but folks from language and other areas, and not being able to make heads or tails of the language part of the work. At least in discussions at the time, they were fairly heavy with lingo within the area and just seemed so far from stuff I was comfortable with. I just never bothered to really get into it.

For better or worse, everyone's paying attention now, and hopefully we're not doing it too badly. Folks that know, either linguists or core NLP people, sometimes complain about how the rest of machine learning engages in some of their research, but hopefully they would agree that some of our contributions are positively affecting language specifically.

items.question: How do you understand the interest and concern around apparent emergent abilities in large language models?
items.object: Apparent emergent abilities in large language models
items.answer:
Some of our colleagues had observed what they called emergence: this observation that on some tasks, some of these large language models seem to be bad when the scale of the model was small and somewhat unpredictably, as you increase scale, would get better. This was the key observation, and just got the name emergence.

A few different potential tasks showed this, but one of the ones that people initially gravitated strongly toward were settings where you're asking the model to add numbers together or do various kinds of simple arithmetic. One reason there was a lot of interest in this application was the hypothesis that the ability to do arithmetic is tied to some aspects of reasoning. This idea that models could do reasoning is quite fundamental to the potential of, in the future, having models, on the positive side, implement or run more important aspects, or just do more important things, and the maybe more concerning side, potential adverse outcomes if these models get good in a way that people don't have a handle on.

This is some of the discussion in the ether, broadly within the space, because of this observation of what seems to be an abrupt change, most importantly unpredictable abrupt change. That was the aspect that people seemed most concerned with: you don't know what scale the model seems to get better.

items.question: What do you think machine learning researchers need to examine more carefully about their choice of evaluation metrics?

items.answer: I've spent a huge chunk of my career talking about metrics and trying to convince my colleagues to spend more time thinking more carefully about metrics. items.question: How do you use your coin-toss toy model to examine claims that emergent language-model behavior is unpredictable?
items.object: A coin-toss toy model for examining the apparent unpredictability of emergent language-model behavior
items.answer:
Probably the most interesting bit for me is both the fact that you have this sharp behavior, which is interesting, and the unpredictability of it, which is also interesting. I think we can make a somewhat stronger argument to counter at least some of the discussion happening.

We posited a very simple toy model, admittedly toy in that it ignores a lot of what we think language models are doing and simply considers language models as next-word predictors, so next-token predictors. We take the actual training objective at face value. More than that, we ignore even correlations: while predicting a sequence, we just think about this as independent decisions on what the next token should be. So I have a very simple model, if you like, a coin-toss model, where the coin has a parameter that says how likely I am to get the answer right. If this probability is very big, I'm likely to get the answer right for any coin toss. I'm going to do this coin toss in a sequence, and for now I'm going to ignore the fact that, in language, the sequence of tokens I predict are not independent. The whole point of recurrent models, for instance, is that history affects the current prediction, which affects the future. We'll ignore that and just think about this as coin toss.

It turns out this somewhat abstract simplification is sufficient to capture a lot of qualitative properties about what metrics might do. You can characterize this very simple model quite precisely and do a bunch of math with it. In particular, you can work out what you expect to happen as I change the probability of success: if I change the probability of getting an answer right, what do I expect to happen if I'm measuring the number of times I get a sequence correct? This allows us to reframe the addition question as: how likely am I to get four or five numbers correct in a row? I'm ignoring the fact that I'm actually doing addition; I'm just thinking, I'm going to pick the next token, will I get the right next token, right or wrong? We have some sense of what we expect models to do because existing work on scaling laws, these empirical observations of what cross-entropy looks like as I increase models, gives us a handle on roughly what's the average probability that you get the next token right. That's something like what cross-entropy is measuring.

items.question: How do you see a simple fixed-probability model helping explain the emergence curve in language-model accuracy?
items.object: A fixed-probability model of getting five consecutive tokens correct
items.answer: Let's say five tokens in a row correct. This is a kind of question I would give to a probability class as homework, but I don't say this in a dismissive way to any of the claims I've made. I'm mostly, again, saying this is a simple model, but it's simple enough to illustrate the point quite clearly. It's a question I might ask a probability class: how likely am I to get five answers in a row correct if I have some sort of known probability of getting one answer correct? Roughly, if I make a mistake in the first one, then I'm done; I might get the first one correct, or make a mistake in the second one, then I'm done. If you do this, you see a curve that looks notoriously like the emergence curve. This overall accuracy measure changes from close to zero to close to one; it's perfectly predicted.

items.question: How do you understand the S-shaped emergence curve in arithmetic tasks through your simple probability model?

items.answer: Our results, while on this very simple toy model, match or predict the observed data quite well. If you look at arithmetic problems and the number of tokens I need to get, say, five plus five or four-digit addition right, you generally need to get five tokens correct, because four digits, and then often there'll be something that will roll over if the numbers are big enough. If I just plot with this very simple model, assuming there's some fixed number that tells me how likely I am to get the first token right, second token right, third token right, fourth token right, and so forth, what should I expect to see in terms of overall probability that I get all five tokens correct? items.question: How do you see the choice of reconstruction metric shaping the apparent progress of an autoencoder?
items.object: Threshold-based evaluation of autoencoder reconstruction
items.answer: We looked at autoencoders, models useful for summarizing data. They find low-dimensional embeddings of data so that you can compress large data sets in low-dimensional space. They're useful for denoising and compression. A big part of the field is building good autoencoders, and people use them inside much larger models that do fancy stuff. We looked at autoencoders, usually measured by some metric that says how close my predicted image is to the original image, how well did I reconstruct a particular image. This is generally something like a squared loss or something in that family, some kind of norm. We replace this with a measure that gives you full credit if you're within a small value close to the perfect reconstruction, and zero credit if you're far away. So instead of seeing the model getting better slowly, you're seeing the model is far away, no credit.

items.question: How do you see DecodingTrust’s role in evaluating the trustworthiness of language models?

We landed on eight perspectives. These included toxicity, stereotype bias, robustness of different kinds, privacy, ethics, and fairness. For each of these, we came up with some evaluation, some way to query models and get a response, and then evaluate this to give us some signal about how well the model might be doing with respect to various trustworthiness measures. We applied these to a bunch of different models. The main task was designing this evaluation and figuring out how to make sure things were scalable. For some directions we had to come up with new metrics; for others we extended existing metrics to be more flexible and have better coverage of various aspects of model behavior.

In the end, we have this toolbox that has a GitHub page and is also on Hugging Face, so people can easily download and run the evaluation. We're hoping to build this up quite a bit, and in the long term have a big suite of evaluations for model behavior that builds on excellent work by our colleagues on evaluation for performance. There's a bunch of work on performance evaluations, notably my colleague Percy Liang and colleagues, who have HELM out of Stanford, widely used for people thinking about evaluating performance of language models. We noticed the gap that the group thought was important, directions related to trustworthiness that we wanted to try to help fill.

items.question: How do you think about the appropriate level of generality for model evaluation in work such as DecodingTrust?
items.object: General-purpose model evaluation and DecodingTrust
items.answer: A version of this question I've been thinking about a lot recently is what level of general purpose is the right level of abstraction to think about evaluation for models. A lot of the evaluation stack thinks about models mostly user-facing, in that the user can ask anything, and thinks about what we might evaluate. There's a coverage problem, maybe, but it's tricky because there's lots of flexibility in the potential interaction. I'd argue perhaps that a lot of the existing work, but also this DecodingTrust work, is targeted at that general use case in that way. Ignoring coverage for a second, because I think that's a meaningful caveat, I'd argue that all the instances of tests we come up with are interactions that either there's evidence for or simple thought experiments. It's not a stretch to have people interact with a model for various kinds of decision-making settings, or query it for some outcome where we want to be careful about bias in various ways or security leakage, for instance.

items.question: How do you think about evaluating whether language models are ready for use in health care and education?
items.object: Domain-specific evaluation of language models in health care and education
items.answer: I've been talking quite a bit to various domains, most importantly and recently to folks in health care who are either thinking of deploying or already deploying language models, either clinician-facing or sometimes patient-facing—clinician decision support or triage sometimes, or patient-facing to maybe do some early screening. For better or worse, these things are here, and there's a lot of interest in potentially using them. There's a question of how can we tell whether we think these models are ready for prime time in these settings? Similarly for education. items.question: How do you think health care changes the way you can evaluate harm from language models?
items.object: Evaluating harm from language models in health care
items.answer: For something like health care, I think something very specific—actually both health care and education—the notion of harm often has much clearer resolution. I think harm can be vaguer in the general-purpose sense. In health care, if I have a recommendation for treatment and known drug interactions that are fatal, or I have someone I'm recommending something to and the actual recommendation will kill the person, the harm there is just very clear and obvious. I think that clarifies gaps at least at some level and suggests some evaluation mechanisms you may not be thinking about as clearly if you're thinking about general-purpose use, because you'd imagine people are not using it for medical decision-making settings.

items.question: How do you think language-model evaluations should adapt to the particular contexts in which people use them?
items.object: Context-specific evaluation of language models
items.answer:
Thinking about exactly how to build evaluations that can capture all these has been tricky. Where I hope we will go, and some of what we're building and working towards, is a path where we can get good at having a very large suite of possible evaluation tests and then pull which subsets of these are relevant for a particular context. A context might be particular domains. Health care itself is huge: there are specific specialties; they all have specific interests. Cardiology and radiology care about often different things. In fact, as an aside, often issues with health care come from the fact that there are competing interests for the different specialties and what they think is most important in your care. That's an aside, but it brings up challenging questions on how to think about evaluation and at what level of abstraction or what level of use: general domains, specialties, individual hospitals, individual doctors or clinicians. I'm optimistic about the route where we can build a large enough suite of tests that the work becomes what to pull for a specific context.

I think there's some interesting work in personalization, said broadly, but specialization of tests. Are there ways to semi-automatically figure out what subsets of a large suite of tests are most relevant to a particular individual, maybe tied to their values? Some colleagues have been playing around a little bit and understanding better how people's values affect how they interface with technology. Maybe there's space to capture some of that and how we think about tests at different levels of abstraction. It's a hard one. As a general statement, yes, I think we're building tests that we think are relevant for practice. As a specific statement, I think there's still some gap in what practice means.

items.object: Evaluating individual tools within LLM systems
items.answer: I think there's space to think about how to evaluate all of these tools separately, which could be interesting because it allows for interesting use cases of being able to mix and match. items.question: Where do you see gaps in prompt-based LLM evaluations such as DecodingTrust?
items.object: Transparency and data contamination in prompt-based LLM evaluations
items.answer: At least for DecodingTrust and similar evaluations, they all purely prompt, so in some sense they only care about input and output from the point of view of the test. They're testing the system, whatever the system is. Because of this there's probably some coverage gaps. There are parts of evaluation that are tricky to do without transparency. There are meaningful gaps in understanding, for instance, training data, because we know it affects models in particular ways. There's a line of work some of my other students are playing with that I also find very interesting, thinking about data contamination. This is a big issue in evaluations and tests, as you might know, because, one, many of the tests have data sources that are effectively online because they're open tests, by design, so people can use them. This is not a statement or an accusation, but it's just an observation: if I'm building a model, the obvious thing for me to do is to train my model on the test because I'll look really good with respect to that test data. The incentives are set up that way. I have no evidence anyone is doing anything; I'm just observing that this is a problem.
